Coincidentally, the Numba team also tried building Numba on ppc64le a few weeks ago and saw similar failures, but we don't understand the root cause.  We conjectured it had to do with atomic reference counting behavior on ppc64le that is different than x86, but that doesn't seem to be the whole story.

Also, thanks for the reminder about the requirements.txt.  You've caught us in the middle of our release process when we are tagging new releases.

At this point, I don't think we have any.  Make sure you are using the final Numba 0.34 release, as that includes a patch to fix a race condition in LLVM initialization that was causing problems on x86.

Basically, @stuartarchibald was seeing a few different problems with Numba:
 * Our atomic reference counting implementation assumes the x86 memory model, and POWER has weaker consistency rules between cores by default.  We tried changing the code we generated to compensate, but the result was *much* slower and still segfaulted.
* Tests involving complex numbers are failing, and this may be due to differences in how they are laid out in memory, but we have not confirmed that.
* The exp() function seems to be giving different answers than we expect, but that may be unrelated.
Most of the segfaults are appearing when the Python GIL is being reacquired, which we also find confusing.

Unfortunately, we don't have resources at this point to chase the issue further.  We would very much like to support POWER8, though.

There are numerous difficult problems afflicting Numba on PowerPC:

- The atomic increment/decrement was not fenced correctly; In fact it wasn't fenced at all. I've chosen the most lightweight fencing that will render safe the generated atomic reference increment and decrement functions. This is taken care of in my PRs.

- The above is just 10% of the problems. 90% of all problems are due to _**awful**_ JIT relocation.
  - The JIT puts enormous gaps between some JITed modules, in some cases as much as 8GB. This causes LLVM build in Debug mode to abort when it fails to relocate `R_PPC64_REL32` relocations with a displacement of range only `[-2**31, 2**31-1]`. The partial solution is to use the `large` code model. This solves a lot of testcase segfaults as well. It's included in the Numba PR as well.

### Speculation

I'm still speculating as to why that might happen. I notice that Object 3's and Object 4's TOC layouts are not compatible; Indeed, the wrapper function's TOC entries were prepended to the TOC rather than appended. Further, the `.text` TOC relocations of `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` are consistent with Object 3, while the `.text` TOC relocations of `__gufunc__._ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` are consistent with Object 4. I also notice that Object 3 and 4 share definitions: They share the definition of `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` and all TOC entries it required, although in Object 4 the definition of `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` has `weak` linkage.

My best guess is that Object 3 was JITed to memory before Object 4, and Object 4 doesn't manage to fully supplant Object 3. Instead, Object 3 and 4 hybridize, with Object 4 losing against Object 3 over `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` due to having the weaker definition of the two. Unfortunately I'm not an expert in either Numba or LLVM's architecture, so I do not know whether this was Numba's intent, or whether it is permissible in LLVM `MCJIT`. I will ponder these questions some more and continue hacking away.

### Conclusion

It appears to me that codegen is flawless. Exactly the right relocatable code and relocatable object files are generated, and they would run perfectly if they were properly relocated.

- *The mistake is not in codegen.*
- *The mistake happens approximately at JIT relocation time.*
- *The mistake happens no sooner than the invocation of* `RuntimeDyldImpl::loadObjectImpl()` *and no later than the invocations of* `RuntimeDyldELF::resolveRelocation()` *when Numba invokes* `MCJIT::finalizeObject()`.
- *The mistake may involve unintentional hybridizing of JITed objects*.
- *The mistake may involve* `weak` *definitions*.

I am now convinced that this is an issue at the intersection of function linkage and TOC relocations. The following is a one-liner change that seems to avoid all segfaults (But _don't apply it!_):

```diff
diff --git a/numba/targets/codegen.py b/numba/targets/codegen.py
index 076c900..c2d42cc 100644
--- a/numba/targets/codegen.py
+++ b/numba/targets/codegen.py
@@ -154,7 +154,7 @@ class CodeLibrary(object):
             for name in to_fix:
                 # NOTE: this will mark the symbol WEAK if serialized
                 # to an ELF file
-                mod.get_function(name).linkage = 'linkonce_odr'
+                mod.get_function(name).linkage = 'available_externally'
         self._shared_module = mod
         return mod
```

_How I intuited this:_

- I knew already that the PPC64 ABI requires that the `r2` point to the base of the TOC table + `0x8000` bytes. Typically, the first two instructions after a function's entry point ensure this. If the `r2` pointer is already known to be set properly (e.g. because an intra-module call is being performed), then one may optimize by jumping directly to the LEP (Local Entry Point) of the function, just past the code that sets up `r2`.
- I noticed that a few bytes after `__gufunc__._ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei`, there began a copy of `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` that was correctly relocated _(TOC relocations consistent with Object 4!!!)_, but it wasn't being used (because the name `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` mapped to Object 3's strongly-defined copy, so the call in Object 4's `__gufunc__._ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` to a function called `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` went to Object 3's copy of it, leaving the Object 4 copy lurking in darkness).
- I carefully considered that TOC relocations for already-emitted objects cannot be redone/moved once they go _live_ (the code pages are marked executable/read-only for security purposes).
- But Object 3 and 4 have incompatible TOC table layouts, so they cannot share their TOC table. They must use two separate ones, and speak to each other as if between strangers (including setting the `r2` TOC pointer register properly in calls between themselves).
- Yet that is not what was happening. Object 4 was build as a single module containing

    1) A strong definition of `__gufunc__._ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` and
    2) A `linkonce_odr` definition of `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei`.

  and **the intra-module call from the former to the later used the LEP (Local Entry Point) at** `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei+8`. Therefore, when Object 3's `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` subsequently won over Object 4's `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei`, **an Object 4 intra-module call became an Object 4->3 inter-module call requiring the setting of `r2`.**

  Due to the failure to set `r2` properly, **the Object 3 `_ZN8__main__7foo$241Ei` used Object 4's `r2` TOC pointer, and thus read the wrong table for global variable addresses!!!**.
- I was bothered by that line of code that set `linkonce_odr`, which marked it `weak` in the object generated by MCJIT and thus permitted relaxation of intra-module calls. I looked at LLVM's Language Reference and found that [`available_externally`](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#linkage-types) seemed to both put appropriate distance between the modules and yet at the same time give the compiler the knowledge required for optimization. I tried it out and it sure seems to have worked.

This is probably not, I repeat, **not** a proper solution, but I believe I have unearthed the root cause of all those segfaults and that we may now properly treat it.

Based on that, and obilaniu's reproduction of the failure llvm-rtdyld my current speculation is this (I have not verified this in the RuntimeDyldELF code yet):

RuntimeDyld is tracking the local function entry points only in its symbol table. Earlier versions of RuntimeDyld overwrote the symbol table entries for ODR functions (meaning calls always linked against the most recently emitted copy of the callee). The change to discard redundant weak symbol definitions means that all calls are now linked to the first copy of the callee that was emitted. The weak symbol resolution fix is the right thing to do in order to match LLVM linkage semantics. I think the correct fix for RuntimeDyld is to have it recognize when it is calling a function with a different TOC and switch to calling it via the external entry point.

@lhames You are correct: Functions have two entry points: a **GEP** that contains code that sets `r2` to the right value no matter what it was before, which falls through to the **LEP**, that assumes `r2` is already set correctly. Intra-module calls can call directly into the LEP on the assumption that because they share their `r2`, they need not set it again to the same value.

I believe that `RuntimeDyld`'s current behaviour of only keeping the first copy of the callee that is emitted is _correct_; Once it's emitted and loaded, the pointer to it may be passed off to some other thread that's concurrently executing that code (and may be waiting inside it), so it must not be touched or moved.

A TOC table is produced 0 or more times per object file loaded into the execution engine. You may inspect it with `objdump` and `readelf` looking at the section `.rela.toc`. In the minimal reproduction example I gave above, `Module1.o`'s `.rela.toc` has one entry (a pointer to `11.0`) and `Module2.o`'s has two entries (a pointer to `17.0` and then a pointer to `11.0`).

Thanks for the info @obilaniu, that's very useful to know. Ultimately, we wrote the PPCCTRLoops pass to insert these intrinsics in IR presumably because of the availability of useful analyses such as SCEV. I imagine that the use case of feeding this IR back through the optimizer never occurred to anyone. However, target intrinsics in IR are not all that uncommon (clang's codegen will insert a bunch - certainly on PPC). It just means that we have to carefully evaluate what properties these intrinsics have (in retrospect, non-duplicability probably should have been an obvious one because BDZ/BDNZ one is implicit control flow).

Loops using the count register are generally faster than those based on comparisons and control flow, so disabling the pass is probably not profitable (as long as we can verify the bugs are fixed).
